newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Burmese leader arrives for S.E. Asian summit.
newsitem.headline: Burmese leader arrives for S.E. Asian summit.

text.p: The head of Burma's military government arrived in Jakarta on Thursday for a one-day summit meeting of Southeast Asian nations amid growing speculation on when his country will be allowed to join the ASEAN grouping.
General Than Shwe, accompanied by military intelligence chief Lieutenant-General Khin Nyunt and six members of the cabinet, arrived on a special flight from Rangoon.
Saturday's meeting of the heads of government of the seven-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations will also be attended by Burma, Cambodia and Laos as observers.
Than Shwe said in a statement issued on his arrival that his visit "reaffirmed the sincere desire of the government and people of Myanmar (Burma) to integrate themselves into ASEAN".
He said he would use the summit "to renew personal contacts and exchange views with other heads of government".

While Cambodia and Laos are on track to become full-fledged members of ASEAN next year, Burma's case has been dogged by its crackdown on the pro-democracy movement led by Nobel peace laureate Aung San Suu Kyi.

ASEAN, which groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam, has been under intense pressure from Western nations and human rights activists to delay admitting Rangoon because of the crackdown.

In the past month, cracks have appeared in ASEAN's stand that it will not respond to external pressures on the membership issue. Some leaders have publicly expressed reservations on admitting Burma as a full member in 1997.
But Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas told reporters on Wednesday that no ASEAN members opposed the entry of Burma.
"In principle, the entry of Myanmar into ASEAN poses no problems to ASEAN. All ASEAN members are agreed that Myanmar needs to enter, needs to be accepted as a member," he said.
Diplomatic sources said it was not a question of whether Burma would be admitted, but of when.
In Rangoon, the official media accused the United States of trying to divide ASEAN over the Burma issue.

Using the word "Ngapwagyi" -- loosely translated as "trouble maker" -- for the United States, a commentary in all three state-run newspapers said: "Whether Myanmar is accepted as an ASEAN member or not is not a matter for Ngapwagyi..."

"It is an evil and dirty plot of Ngapwagyi, hitting the vulnerable spot to hinder Myanmar's wish to enter ASEAN and to make ASEAN nations become disunited. Ngapwagyi is implementing this scheme with all-out efforts," the commentary said.
On a visit to Thailand earlier this week, U.S. President Bill Clinton criticised the Burmese government's policies.

In a speech praising most Asia-Pacific nations for their efforts to bring democracy to the region, Clinton singled out Burma for failing to recognise a democratically elected government, saying it showed Rangoon lacked rule of law.
In Jakarta, meanwhile, there were other problems associated with observer nations at the summit.

Cambodian Embassy officials said both First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Second Prime Minister Hun Sen would attend the summit. The two, who have been squabbling in recent weeks, were arriving separately.
"Other countries have only one prime minister. We have two, so both are coming," said one embassy official.
